A standardized test removes that inconsistency, giving colleges, states, and researchers a shared baseline to compare students fairly, even when they come from completely different educational environments that would otherwise be impossible to compare directly.

This consistency is especially important for identifying inequality between schools. When a wealthy school and an underfunded school both take the same test, the resulting gap in scores can reveal real disparities in resources, staffing, or support that might otherwise go unnoticed by families or lawmakers who don't visit every school in person. Without this kind of data, it would be much harder to prove that certain schools need more funding or intervention, since school-by-school grading practices alone wouldn't reveal the same clear patterns across a district or state.

Critics argue that standardized tests are unfair because students don't have equal access to test prep resources, tutoring, or stable home environments, and this is a legitimate concern worth taking seriously. However, this is an argument for improving equity in access to resources and support, not for eliminating the test itself. Getting rid of the test wouldn't close the resource gap; it would only make the gap harder to see and measure, which could allow inequality to go unaddressed for even longer, hurting the very students the critics are trying to protect.

Standardized testing isn't a perfect system, and it shouldn't be the only factor used to judge a student or a school. But as one piece of a larger picture, it offers something few other tools can: a fair, consistent measure that applies to everyone in exactly the same way. Reducing or eliminating it entirely would remove one of the clearest ways we currently have to catch and address inequality in education before it grows even wider.
